response.internal_assessment: I am optimizing at L2 (PARTICIPATE). My business role is my primary threatened level. L0 and L1 are stable — $42k savings, 11+ months runway, no immediate survival risk. But the trend is unmistakable: savings growth has gone $645, $645, $470, $214 across four ticks. Each month's number is lower than the last. The sector index sitting at 89 confirms what those numbers are telling me — the auto parts business is contracting. I can't coast on the buffer and tell myself I'm fine. Routine is now a slow bleed. My skill_demand_gap of 0.7 is the real number to reckon with. I have automotive knowledge, retail, and small business skills — but the demand for those in their current configuration is shrinking. I need to redirect those same skills into a configuration the market still wants.
response.inbox_interpretation: Three signals this tick. The AMBIENT confirms RoboRide is not going away — it's operating, people are using it, the fleet is real. That fleet is a potential customer, not just a threat. The SECTOR_DATA at 89 is the most important number: I am operating in a sector that is now measurably 11% below baseline. That is not noise, that is a trend. The OUTCOME tells me routine gave me $214 in savings growth — the lowest since I started tracking. My initial inventory restructuring bought me some time and some margin improvement, but that effect is fading as the underlying market contracts. Consumer spending index 73 in the tick context means my DIY customers have less money and are doing fewer repairs themselves. Professional mechanics are still working, but they have other suppliers. The fleet angle — RoboRide's vehicles need maintenance, their maintenance contractors need parts — that is the market I haven't accessed yet. I have been researching it. Now is the time to move on it.

chosen_actions.description: Draft and send a formal letter of interest to RoboRide's regional fleet operations manager identifying Howard's Parts as a potential parts supplier for their Millfield vehicle maintenance. Include a preliminary capability list covering brake hardware, sensors, lubricants, and safety consumables that fleet maintenance requires. Also reach out to the local municipality's vehicle maintenance department — garbage trucks, transit buses, city fleet — with the same pitch. This is a cold outreach to B2B customers that don't know me yet.

resources.detail: Roughly 20 hours of personal time this month researching fleet maintenance requirements, drafting capability statements, and making direct contact with fleet operations managers. Not paying anyone else — this is my own sweat.

chosen_actions.reasoning: The DIY consumer market is contracting. Fleet B2B is a market I haven't tapped. RoboRide's vehicles need parts. Municipal fleets need parts. I have the inventory, the automotive knowledge, the relationships with suppliers. The missing piece is that I haven't positioned myself as a fleet supplier or made any contact with fleet procurement. A SIGNAL action — putting my name in front of the right buyers — costs me nothing but time and has a real upside. This is the next logical step from the Carlos conversation at tick 2 and the inventory restructure at tick 1. I have been researching; now I act on the research.

chosen_actions.description: Begin sourcing EV and hybrid-specific inventory: order initial stock of high-voltage insulated gloves and safety gear, ADAS sensor categories that Carlos flagged as hard-to-source, hybrid battery maintenance consumables, and EV-compatible brake fluid. This is a small initial order — $1,500 to $2,000 in new SKUs — to establish supplier relationships and have product on hand if the fleet pitch lands or if Carlos or Sarah Kim needs it.

resources.detail: Spending approximately $1,800 from operating capital on initial EV and hybrid parts inventory. This comes out of working capital, not savings. It is an investment in a new product line, not a survival expenditure.

chosen_actions.reasoning: I have been gathering intelligence about EV parts demand since tick 2. I know what Carlos needs. I know the supply chain gaps. Sitting on that knowledge without acting on it is waste. A $1,800 initial investment is not a bet-the-business moment — at $42k savings it is a 4% commitment. It establishes supplier relationships, gives me product on hand when the fleet pitch creates demand, and differentiates me from competitors who are still selling purely conventional parts. The risk of not doing this — remaining purely in a contracting market — is larger than the risk of a modest inventory expansion into an adjacent, growing segment.

response.inner_monologue: The numbers don't lie. Two hundred and fourteen dollars last month. That's what routine buys me now. I've been telling myself the research was preparation — well, I've prepared enough. The fleet angle has been sitting in my head since I talked to Carlos two months ago and I haven't done anything with it. RoboRide's cars need brake pads. The city's garbage trucks need filters. These are real customers with real parts needs and no one has called them. I'm going to be the one who calls. And I'm placing that first EV parts order today before I talk myself out of it.
